title: Einstein’s Postulates
lead: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame of reference, and the speed of light $\kc$ in a vacuum is the same for every observer, whatever the motion of its source. The second cannot be squared with Newton’s addition of velocities, and the Michelson-Morley experiment is the evidence for it.
objectives: State and explain both of Einstein’s postulates.
Explain what an inertial frame of reference is.
Describe one way the speed of light can be changed.
summary_html:
• Relativity is the study of how different observers measure the same event.
  • Modern relativity is divided into two parts. Special relativity deals with observers who are in uniform (unaccelerated) motion, whereas general relativity includes accelerated relative motion and gravity. Modern relativity is correct in all circumstances and, in the limit of low velocity and weak gravitation, gives the same predictions as classical relativity.
  • An inertial frame of reference is a reference frame in which a body at rest remains at rest and a body in motion moves at a constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by an outside force.
  • Modern relativity is based on Einstein’s two postulates. The first postulate of special relativity is the idea that the laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference. The second postulate of special relativity is the idea that the speed of light $\kc$ is a constant, independent of the relative motion of the source.
  • The Michelson-Morley experiment demonstrated that the speed of light in a vacuum is independent of the motion of the Earth about the Sun.

exercises.prompt: Explain how special relativity differs from general relativity.

answer.solution: Special relativity applies only to unaccelerated motion, but general relativity applies to accelerated motion.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements describes the Michelson-Morley experiment?

options: The speed of light is independent of the motion of the source relative to the observer.
The speed of light is different in different frames of reference.
The speed of light changes with changes in the observer.
The speed of light is dependent on the motion of the source.
answer.hint: The experiment looked for a change in the speed of light as the Earth moved about the Sun, and it found none.

exercises.prompt: Which of Einstein’s postulates of special relativity includes a concept that does not fit with the ideas of classical physics? Explain.

answer.solution: The second postulate does. In classical physics velocities add like simple vectors, so an observer moving toward a source of light should measure the light moving faster than an observer at rest, and one moving away should measure it moving slower. The second postulate says that every observer measures the same speed $\kc$, whatever the relative motion of the source, which Newton’s addition of velocities cannot allow. The first postulate, that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, was already true of Newton’s laws.

exercises.prompt: Is Earth an inertial frame of reference? Is the Sun? Justify your response.

answer.solution: Strictly, neither is. The Earth rotates on its axis and moves in a curved orbit about the Sun, so it is accelerated, and the Sun itself orbits the center of the galaxy. An inertial frame must be neither accelerated nor rotating. Both are nearly inertial for many purposes, since their accelerations are small, and the Sun is closer to an inertial frame than the Earth is, because its acceleration is much smaller.

exercises.prompt: When you are flying in a commercial jet, it may appear to you that the airplane is stationary and the Earth is moving beneath you. Is this point of view valid? Discuss briefly.

answer.solution: Yes, as long as the plane flies at a constant altitude and speed in a straight line. Then the plane is, very nearly, an inertial frame, and by the first postulate the laws of physics are the same in it as on the ground. There is no preferred frame and no absolute motion, so saying the Earth moves beneath a stationary plane is as valid as saying the plane moves over a stationary Earth. The view breaks down while the plane takes off, lands or turns, because it is then accelerated and fictitious forces appear.
